title: Testing Asymmetric-Information Asset Pricing Models
research_question: Does information asymmetry among investors have a substantial effect on equilibrium stock prices and investor demands, and if so, through what channel does it operate? Specifically, how do increases (or decreases) in the degree of information asymmetry about a stock affect its price, the holdings of institutional versus retail investors, and its exposure to liquidity risk?
data_description: The authors compile a sample of 4,429 stock-level analyst coverage terminations affecting 2,180 unique U.S. firms, generated by 43 brokerage firms closing their U.S. equity research operations between Q1 2000 and Q1 2008. They also use 356 terminations from two brokers devastated by the 9/11 attacks and 1,019 coverage reinitiations (902 firms, Q4 1997–Q1 2008) following mergers between retail and institutional brokers. Analyst coverage data come from Reuters Estimates, I/B/E/S, and Investext termination notices; stock returns and prices from CRSP; accounting data from Compustat; institutional ownership from Thomson Reuters CDA/Spectrum 13f filings; and analyst forecasts/earnings from I/B/E/S. Variables include daily stock returns, bid-ask spreads, Amihud illiquidity, turnover, earnings surprises, analyst characteristics (location, all-star rating, experience), and quarterly institutional holdings. The unit of observation is a stock-event (or stock-quarter for demand tests).
institutional_context: The setting exploits a wave of exits from sell-side equity research in the United States during the 2000s. Following the 2000–2003 bear market, declining trading commissions, SEC scrutiny of soft-dollar arrangements, and post-Global-Settlement restrictions on cross-subsidies from investment banking, 43 brokerage firms shut their research departments between 2000 and early 2008, abruptly terminating analyst coverage of thousands of stocks for reasons unrelated to the prospects of any specific covered firm. A second setting arises from the September 11, 2001 attacks, which killed analysts at Keefe, Bruyette & Woods and Sandler O'Neill and forced involuntary coverage drops. A third setting involves mergers in which retail brokerages acquired institutional brokerages, making research previously confined to institutional clients newly available to retail investors. Sell-side analysts are key information producers, and retail investors rely heavily on their public reports while institutions can produce private signals in-house.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The study finds that asymmetric-information asset pricing models do not adequately explain asset returns during periods of high information asymmetry.
